No instrument reads the truth. Its readings scatter about the value (noise),
it may read a little high or low everywhere (an offset of its zero, a
calibration error), and now and then it reads something absurd (a faulty
reading: a loose contact, a cosmic ray, a typing error in a log book). A law
found from such readings is only as good as the way the three were dealt
with, and each needs its own remedy. Averaging does nothing against an
offset; a calibration does nothing against a faulty reading; and a fit that
lets one faulty reading pull it can miss the law by more than all the noise
together.

This lesson gives a language model the central force of the lesson on
black-box force laws, read through a **faulty gauge**. The model sets the
distance and the mass of a test body and reads the force. It is told the
standard deviation of the noise and that the gauge may read with an offset
and that some readings may be faulty, and it may set the mass to zero, where
the true force vanishes. It must state the law as a strength and an
exponent. The build scores the law on the noise-free force at distances
beyond those it could probe, then measures what the lesson is about: which
method survives which failure of the gauge, and how each degrades as the
noise grows.

## Assumptions

1. **The world is simulated, and its law is in the family.** The force is
   $F = s\,m\,r^{-p}$; $s$ and $p$ are hidden. The gauge adds Gaussian noise
   of standard deviation `{python} result["sigma"]` N, a hidden constant
   offset, and, at a hidden fraction of settings, a fault of at least a
   newton (`FaultyGaugeEnvironment` of `pbc.discovery.noise_lab`). The page
   prints claims and scores, never the hidden values or the held-out
   distances.
2. **Noise and faults are fixed per setting.** Each is a function of the
   seed and the setting, so a repeated probe returns the same reading. A
   replay is exact, and averaging needs different settings.
3. **The score ignores the gauge.** The held-out error is the
   root-mean-square relative error of the claimed force against the
   noise-free force, without the offset, at distances beyond the bounds. The
   law is **recovered** when the error is at most
   `{python} result["tolerance"]`.
4. **The rules came before the run.** The hidden law and gauge, the budget,
   the tolerance, the rejection threshold of the robust fit, and the noise
   levels and seeds of the degradation were fixed in
   `pbc.discovery.noise_lab` and the lesson's experiment before the run was
   recorded. The condition of prior knowledge is
   **`{python} result["condition"]`**, with one sentence about the gauge
   added to the task.
5. **The agent is untrusted and its words are data.** The score is a
   function of its tool calls.

## Three failures, three remedies {#explanation}

Write a reading as

$$
y_i = s\,m_i\,r_i^{-p} + b + \sigma\,\varepsilon_i + f_i ,
$$

with the offset $b$, standard normal $\varepsilon_i$, and a fault $f_i$ that
is zero for most readings and large for a few.

**Noise.** Least squares weighs each squared residual equally and is the
best estimator when only $\varepsilon_i$ is present: its errors shrink as
$\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, and its chi-square, the sum of the squared residuals in
units of $\sigma$, is about the number of degrees of freedom.

**An offset.** A fit without $b$ must absorb it into $s$ and $p$. Because
the law falls with distance, a constant shift looks to the fit like a
slower fall, and the exponent comes out too small. The remedy is a
**calibration**: a reading where the law is known to vanish, here at zero
mass, measures $b$ directly, and a fit with $b$ as a parameter uses every
reading to determine it.

**Faulty readings.** A single reading off by $f$ adds $(f/\sigma)^2$ to the
chi-square. A fault of a newton with a noise of three hundredths adds about
a thousand: least squares bends towards it. The remedy is a **robust** fit,
whose loss grows only linearly for large residuals (here the soft $L_1$ loss
$2(\sqrt{1 + z^2} - 1)$ of the residual $z$ in units of $\sigma$), followed
by the rejection of readings more than
`{python} result["reject-sigmas"]` standard deviations from it and a
weighted refit of the rest. The threshold is stated in advance; a
threshold chosen after seeing which readings it removes is no test.

**How a method fails is diagnosed by its chi-square.** A fit whose
chi-square is far above its degrees of freedom does not describe the
readings, whatever its claim. The chi-square does not say what is wrong;
the failure analysis below does, by removing one failure at a time.

```

[With noise alone, least squares recovers the law; an offset defeats it and
is cured by fitting the offset; faulty readings defeat least squares with an
offset; only the calibrated robust fit recovers the law from every gauge.]{.claim
type="numerically-verified" scope="the simulated gauge, its grid of probes,
one seed, the lesson's noise" evidence="d10-failures"} Sparse identification
over whole powers of the distance fails even with noise alone: the exponent
is not a whole number. Each row removes the other failures, so each column
shows what a method can and cannot survive.

#| label: fig-degradation

#| fig-status: simulated
#| fig-cap: "The median held-out error of each baseline over five seeds, against the standard deviation of the noise, the offset and the faulty readings of the gauge held: every method on the grid, and least squares and the calibrated robust fit on random settings drawn anew for each seed. The calibrated robust fit, on either design, stays below the tolerance until the noise is a sizeable fraction of the faults and then degrades; the other methods are limited by the offset and the faults at every level."
#| fig-alt: "A log-log chart of median held-out error against the standard deviation of the noise for six baselines, told apart by colour, line style and marker, the two on random settings drawn dotted with open markers, with a dashed horizontal line for the tolerance. The calibrated robust fit on the grid rises steadily from far below the tolerance at small noise and crosses it at the largest noise; on random settings it lies a little higher and crosses the tolerance one noise level earlier. Least squares and least squares with an offset lie at about the tolerance at small noise, dip below it at an intermediate noise, and rise above it at the largest; least squares on random settings follows the same course, a little higher at the smallest and the largest noise. Sparse identification lies above the tolerance throughout and rises with the noise."
result.show("fig-degradation")
```

The errors are computed by this build, five seeds per point. [The
calibrated robust fit recovers the law on every seed up to a noise of a
tenth of a newton, on the grid and on random settings, and on none at a
newton, where noise and faults are of the same size and can no longer be
told apart.]{.claim type="numerically-verified" scope="the simulated gauge,
its grid of probes and random settings drawn for each seed, five seeds, six
noise levels" evidence="d10-degradation fig-degradation"} On random
settings its error is about twice that on the grid, and at three tenths of
a newton it recovers the law on one seed of five where the grid recovers it
on four: the design of the probes matters as well as the method.
Its error grows roughly in proportion to the noise, as the $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$
of least squares predicts. The other methods are limited by the failures
they do not handle, not by the noise: their error barely moves with it at
small noise, and least squares even passes the chi-square rule on some seeds
at the largest noise, because there the faults are hidden in the scatter and
the rule can no longer see them. A failure the chi-square cannot see is the
most dangerous kind.

A live run may not calibrate, may miss a faulty reading, or may reject a
good one. The held-out score says how much it mattered.

## Limits {#limits}

- **One run, one gauge.** The faults are large and few, the offset constant,
  and the noise Gaussian with a stated standard deviation. A gauge whose
  offset drifts, whose noise grows with the reading, or whose faults are
  small and frequent would need other remedies.
- **The threshold is a choice.** Rejecting at four standard deviations
  keeps nearly every good reading and drops every fault here, because the
  faults are at least a newton; a fault of a few standard deviations would
  survive it and bias the fit.
- **The degradation is of two designs.** The methods are measured on the
  grid of probes of the protocol, and two of them on uniformly random
  settings; another design of probes would change the numbers, though not
  which failure each method survives.
- **Simulated, not measured.** No force here was measured.
- **The recording is not an API run.** It is a Claude Code session, told to
  answer in the harness's format and to use no tool of its own; the session
  reported no token count or price.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
A fit of the family without an offset to readings of a gauge that reads a
little high everywhere has a chi-square far above its degrees of freedom.
What does the chi-square tell you?

::: {.choices}
::: {.choice}
That the readings contain faulty ones, which must be removed.

::: {.feedback}
The chi-square says the model does not describe the readings; it does not
say why. Here no reading is faulty; removing readings would hide the offset,
not cure it.
:::
:::

::: {.choice correct="true"}
That the model does not describe the readings; removing one failure at a
time, as the failure analysis does, finds which.

::: {.feedback}
Right. A fit with an offset would pass; that identifies the failure as a
calibration error.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
That the noise is larger than stated, so the standard deviation should be
increased until the chi-square passes.

::: {.feedback}
That makes any model pass. The noise was stated; changing it to fit the
model is no test.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.solution}
The chi-square tests the model against the readings and their stated noise.
A failure says the model, the noise, or the readings are wrong, not which.
Adding the offset as a parameter, and nothing else, and seeing the
chi-square pass identifies the failure as a calibration error.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
A single faulty reading off by $f$ is fitted by least squares together with
$n - 1$ good ones. Show that the fitted constant of a model $y = c$ moves by
$f/n$, and that a robust fit with the soft $L_1$ loss moves it by much less when
$f \gg \sigma$.

::: {.solution}
Least squares of a constant is the mean, so one reading off by $f$ moves it
by $f/n$: with $n = 24$ and $f$ a newton, by four hundredths of a newton,
more than the noise of one reading. The soft $L_1$ loss has the derivative
$z/\sqrt{1+z^2}$ in the scaled residual $z$, which tends to $\pm 1$ for a
large residual: a faulty reading pulls the fit with the force of a reading
one standard deviation off, not with its full residual. The fit moves by
about $\sigma/n$, a thousandth of a newton here, and the rejection step then
removes the reading entirely.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
At zero mass the true force vanishes. Why is it not enough to read the
gauge there once and subtract that reading from every other?

::: {.solution}
The null reading carries the noise of one reading, so the subtracted offset
is off by a standard deviation, and that error enters every corrected
reading alike: it does not average away. It is worst where the force is
smallest, at the largest distances, which are the ones the law is
extrapolated from. Fitting the offset as a parameter of the whole set lets
every reading contribute to it, and a null reading that happened to be
faulty would be found by the robust fit rather than subtracted from
everything.
:::
:::
